Question: A classifier plus a fixed email template is usually better than an agent when:
Option A: The user goal cannot be enumerated
Option B: Every input maps to one of a few known actions
Option C: The next tool depends on unpredictable observations
Option D: You must browse and synthesize many unknown sources

Question: A state machine (graph) agent differs from a free-form ReAct loop because:
Option A: State machines cannot call tools

Option D: Allowed transitions are explicit; the model cannot jump to an arbitrary tool at any time

Question: A tool returns 500. The agent should not:
Option A: Record the error in the trace
Option B: Retry with backoff if the error looks transient and the tool is safe to retry
Option C: Blindly retry in a tight loop with the same side-effecting payload
Option D: Surface a bounded failure to the user after a retry budget

Question: An LLM agent, at minimum, is:
Option A: A single classification head with no tools
Option B: A loop: the model chooses actions (often tool calls), observes results, and continues until it stops
Option C: A database trigger
Option D: A tokenizer with a larger vocabulary

Question: An agent can run `shell` as root on production. What is the actual risk?
Option A: LLMs cannot emit function calls, so the shell tool will never fire.

Option C: Tool calls are sandboxed by default, so the prompt cannot cause harm.

Question: Episodic memory, in agent design, usually means:
Option A: The tokenizer merge table
Option B: GPU scratch space
Option C: Records of past runs or conversations you may retrieve later
Option D: The weights of the base model

Question: For AI agents, a ReAct-style loop thinks, calls a tool, observes, repeats. Why do you still need a max-step budget?
Option A: Without a stop condition the loop can spin (retries, confusion, tool errors) and burn time/money.
Option B: Tools automatically halt after one call.

Question: For AI agents, a step budget or timeout exists so that:
Option A: Retrieval is disabled
Option B: The agent cannot loop until money, time, or tools are exhausted
Option C: Temperature stays at 1
Option D: Memory is encrypted

Question: For AI agents, an over-permissioned tool is dangerous because:
Option A: Permissions only affect logging
Option B: Agents cannot call tools more than once
Option C: The model might call it with a hallucinated argument and actually take the action
Option D: Tools cannot have side effects

Question: For AI agents, retrying a “create payment” tool on timeout is risky unless:
Option A: You raise temperature
Option B: The tool is idempotent or you pass an idempotency key
Option C: You retry as fast as possible
Option D: You hide the error from traces

Question: For AI agents, tool use requires a schema because:
Option A: The model must emit arguments the runtime can parse and validate before execution
Option B: Schemas disable JSON
Option C: Tools ignore types
Option D: Schemas replace authentication

Question: Giving an agent a raw shell tool as “just in case” is a problem because:
Option A: Shells cannot return text
Option B: Models cannot emit command strings
Option C: Timeouts become infinite automatically
Option D: It can run commands you never intended, including destructive or data-exfiltrating ones

Question: If you have no traces, an agent that “sometimes does the wrong tool” is hard to fix because:
Option A: The loop has only one step by definition
Option B: You cannot see the arguments, observations, or which step diverged
Option C: Wrong tools never happen
Option D: Logs are illegal for agents

Question: Traces for agents should record:
Option A: Only GPU temperature
Option B: Only the system prompt, never tool I/O
Option C: Only the final paragraph shown to the user
Option D: Each model step, tool name, arguments, results, and errors, with timings

Question: When is a tool-using agent a worse choice than a plain function call / workflow?
Option A: When you have APIs; agents cannot call APIs.
Option B: Never; agents are always more accurate because they can retry.
Option C: Whenever the task has more than one step.
Option D: When the steps are known, deterministic, and must not invent a plan (refunds, payroll, migrations).

Question: When should you usually not use an agent?
Option A: The user goal is unknown and may need several tools
Option B: You must branch on intermediate observations you cannot precompute
Option C: You need open-ended research with tool use
Option D: The task is a deterministic pipeline or one model call with a known schema

Question: Which is working memory for an agent, not a long-term store?
Option A: A policy wiki in RAG
Option B: A user profile database
Option C: The current prompt: instructions, recent observations, and scratch notes in this run
Option D: A vector index of all past tickets across months

Question: A pipeline writes 10 million 1 KB files to S3 per day. Besides storage bytes, what usually dominates cost and pain?
Option A: ETag computation requires an EC2 instance per object.
Option B: Tiny files cannot be encrypted, so KMS becomes the bottleneck.
Option C: Request (PUT/LIST) charges and slow LIST/rename patterns; many tiny objects are a request-tax design.
Option D: S3 minimum object size is 128 MB, so 1 KB files are rejected.

Question: In AWS / S3, SNS fan-out to multiple SQS queues is useful when:
Option A: You need exactly-once across all consumers without idempotency
Option B: Several independent workers should each see the event; each queue still delivers at-least-once
Option C: S3 becomes a relational store
Option D: Prefix hotspots go away

Question: In AWS / S3, SQS standard queues are at-least-once. Your consumer must:
Option A: Assume each message is processed exactly one time
Option B: Be idempotent; the same message can be delivered more than once
Option C: Use S3 listing as the lock
Option D: Disable checksums

Question: In AWS / S3, a PUT of a new object should include integrity protection by:
Option A: Sending a checksum and verifying it on read; copies plus checksums are the durability story
Option B: Using sequential prefixes
Option C: Storing only in one AZ in the app
Option D: Memorizing a durability percentage

Question: In AWS / S3, durability of an object is achieved by:
Option A: Keeping one copy in the client's browser
Option B: Using SQS as the disk
Option C: A published SLA number you should memorize as the design
Option D: Storing multiple copies and verifying checksums so bit rot and disk loss do not silently win

Question: In AWS / S3, listing a bucket with millions of keys as your 'index' is a bad database because:
Option A: List is transactional
Option B: List is paginated, costly, and not a query planner; you needed a real index or a manifest object
Option C: List returns at-most-once keys
Option D: List evicts objects

Question: In AWS / S3, millions of tiny files (few KB each) get expensive and slow mainly because:
Option A: S3 forbids small objects
Option B: You pay per request and listing/metadata work dominates; throughput is not 'one disk sequential read'
Option C: Checksums fail under 1MB
Option D: Prefixes cannot hold small keys

Question: In AWS / S3, old-style keys like 2024-01-01/log1, 2024-01-01/log2 created prefix hotspots because:
Option A: Dates are invalid key characters
Option B: Many clients hammered the same key prefix/partition at once instead of spreading request load
Option C: S3 cannot store dates
Option D: Checksums collide on dates

Question: In AWS / S3, visibility timeout on SQS exists so that:
Option A: Duplicates are impossible
Option B: Prefixes spread automatically
Option C: Messages become source of truth in S3
Option D: Other consumers hide the message while one works; if you crash, it reappears (at-least-once)

Question: In AWS / S3, why spread entropy in the key (or a hash prefix) for high QPS ingest?
Option A: To disable checksums
Option B: To force at-most-once SQS
Option C: To make listing impossible
Option D: To avoid concentrating request rate on one logical prefix as the workload scales

Question: Putting a database dump on S3 is backup. Using S3 as the live order table is wrong because:
Option A: S3 cannot store bytes
Option B: You lack cheap conditional updates, queries, and low-latency item access as a primary OLTP store
Option C: Checksums disable writes
Option D: Buckets cannot be private

Question: S3 is the wrong place to implement 'query users where lastLogin > X' because:
Option A: S3 deletes data after one day
Option B: Prefixes are strongly transactional
Option C: Objects cannot store JSON
Option D: It is an object store: get-by-key, not a query engine with secondary indexes and predicates

Question: S3 read-after-write for new objects is strongly consistent now. That still does not make S3 a database because:
Option A: You still have no rich queries, joins, or cheap partial updates — only object I/O
Option B: Checksums became optional
Option C: Prefixes became transactions
Option D: Consistency was the only missing SQL feature

Question: Small-file problem on S3 is often fixed by:
Option A: Shorter prefixes only
Option B: Disabling checksums
Option C: One object per database cell
Option D: Batching many logical records into larger objects (and maybe a real database for metadata)

Question: Updating a 'row' in S3 means:
Option A: A Scan of the bucket
Option B: A SQL UPDATE of one field
Option C: Replace the whole object (or write a new version); there is no in-place field update
Option D: A strongly consistent multi-object transaction by default

Question: Why is S3 a poor substitute for a database when you need atomic updates to a JSON blob 100 times a second?
Option A: S3 objects are immutable versions; concurrent writers last-write-win and you have no transactions or secondary indexes.
Option B: S3 cannot store JSON, only images.
Option C: S3 strongly consistent GET still serializes all writes through one global lock, so it is slower but correct.
Option D: S3 will automatically turn the object into DynamoDB after 100 writes.

Question: You put millions of objects under the prefix `logs/2026-09-05/` and request rates spike. What S3 behavior should you design for?
Option A: Very hot prefixes can be rate-limited until S3 scales the keyspace; spread keys (or wait for scaling) rather than hammer one timestamp prefix.
Option B: S3 will shard by file extension automatically.
Option C: You must enable Transfer Acceleration or all PUTs fail.
Option D: S3 has no prefix performance; only bucket name matters.

Question: A service inserts keys uniformly at random. Why does a classic B-tree usually pay more disk writes per insert than an LSM tree?
Option A: LSM trees never fsync and therefore never write
Option B: B-trees store every key in two copies by design
Option C: Each insert can dirty a leaf page (and maybe split), forcing an in-place random page write
Option D: B-trees rewrite the entire tree on every insert

Question: A workload is almost all point lookups and short range scans with in-place updates. Why is a B-tree usually the better default than an LSM tree?
Option A: B-trees do not need a WAL, which removes fsync from the picture.
Option B: B-trees never write more than one page, so they have zero write amplification.
Option C: A B-tree keeps keys ordered on pages you can update in place and scan sequentially; LSM pays compaction and extra reads across levels.
Option D: LSM trees cannot store secondary indexes.

Question: An LSM tree absorbs writes into a memtable and WAL, then flushes sorted runs. What problem is compaction solving?
Option A: It converts the LSM into a B-tree once the dataset fits in RAM.
Option B: It is only used to build secondary indexes; primary key reads skip it.
Option C: It encrypts old runs so they can be deleted from the WAL.
Option D: It merges overlapping sorted runs so reads do not have to search an ever-growing number of files, and it reclaims space from obsolete keys.

Question: For B-trees and LSM trees, a bloom filter returns a false positive for a missing key. What is the user-visible effect?
Option A: Compaction starts immediately
Option B: The engine returns a wrong value
Option C: An extra index/data read of that SSTable that then correctly reports the key absent
Option D: On-disk data is corrupted

Question: For B-trees and LSM trees, after a crash, how is a lost memtable reconstructed?
Option A: Rebuild it from bloom filters
Option B: It cannot be recovered; those writes are gone
Option C: Replay the WAL to rebuild in-memory state
Option D: Scan every SSTable for the newest key

Question: For B-trees and LSM trees, on an LSM point lookup, what does a bloom filter actually tell you?
Option A: Whether the memtable is full
Option B: The exact file offset of the key
Option C: The key is definitely not in this SSTable, or it might be
Option D: Which compaction level owns the key

Question: For B-trees and LSM trees, what does read amplification usually mean for an LSM point get?
Option A: How many replicas must answer
Option B: Bytes written per user write
Option C: How many disk reads or files you may touch to serve one user read
Option D: The size of the WAL in bytes

Question: For B-trees and LSM trees, what happens when a memtable fills under normal LSM operation?
Option A: All older SSTables are deleted immediately
Option B: The WAL is discarded before the flush finishes
Option C: The process blocks until the next restart
Option D: It is frozen, flushed as an immutable SSTable, and a new memtable takes writes

Question: For B-trees and LSM trees, what is the memtable + WAL pair actually buying you in an LSM store?
Option A: Faster range scans than reading SSTables
Option B: A durable crash-recovery log plus a sorted in-memory buffer so acknowledged writes survive a crash
Option C: A replacement for compaction
Option D: A way to skip bloom filters on point lookups

Question: For B-trees and LSM trees, why does making flushed SSTables immutable matter for concurrency?
Option A: The WAL can be skipped
Option B: The memtable can grow without bound
Option C: Old files can still be mutated in place
Option D: Readers can use a file lock-free while a new file is being written elsewhere

Question: For B-trees and LSM trees, why might a single LSM point lookup inspect several SSTables?
Option A: Bloom filters require reading every file
Option B: The WAL must be scanned on every lookup
Option C: Keys are hashed into random files with no order
Option D: The newest version of a key can live in any of several files produced over time

Question: What is compaction's main job in an LSM engine?
Option A: Disable the WAL after the first flush
Option B: Increase write amplification for its own sake
Option C: Merge SSTables, drop obsolete versions and tombstones, and bound how many files a read must check
Option D: Turn the LSM tree into a B-tree

Question: Why are LSM range scans of a key span often heavier than the same scan on a B-tree?
Option A: Range scans always replay the WAL
Option B: Bloom filters block sequential access
Option C: LSM trees cannot iterate keys in sorted order
Option D: You must merge iterators across the memtable and many overlapping SSTables

Question: Why can LSM ingest a flood of random keys faster than a B-tree of similar durable settings?
Option A: B-trees cannot store random keys
Option B: Compaction is free and instantaneous
Option C: User writes append to WAL and memtable instead of randomly updating leaf pages
Option D: LSM engines never fsync

Question: Why do B-trees typically win on short range scans of nearby keys?
Option A: They never split pages
Option B: They attach a bloom filter to every leaf
Option C: They keep all data only in memory
Option D: Leaf pages keep keys in sorted on-disk order with little file overlap, often with sibling links

Question: Why do LSM engines almost always put a Bloom filter in front of each SSTable?
Option A: To skip files that definitely do not contain a key, cutting read amplification on point lookups.
Option B: To make range scans O(1).
Option C: To replace the WAL for crash recovery.
Option D: To compress keys so SSTables fit in RAM.

Question: Write amplification in an LSM tree is dominated by which activity?
Option A: Bloom-filter false positives
Option B: Rewriting the same live data again during compaction
Option C: B-tree page splits
Option D: Replica count in the cluster

Question: In C++, `const std::string& f() { std::string s = "x"; return s; }` What is wrong?
Option A: const references to locals are promoted to static storage.
Option B: The compiler is required to reject this program.
Option C: NRVO extends s to the caller, so the reference is safe.
Option D: You return a reference to a destroyed local; using it is undefined behavior. Return by value.

Question: In C++, `for (unsigned i = n - 1; i >= 0; --i)` with size_t n. Why is this an infinite loop when n is 0 or the last decrement wraps?
Option A: unsigned >= 0 is always true; i wraps to a huge value. Prefer signed indices or a different loop shape.
Option B: The compiler inserts a signed cast around the comparison.
Option C: size_t is signed on LP64, so this cannot wrap.
Option D: unsigned cannot be decremented.

Question: In C++, `std::move` on a local then using it again — what is actually true?
Option A: move copies if the type has a destructor.
Option B: move is a runtime memcpy of the bytes only.
Option C: move guarantees the object is empty and safe to read as 0.
Option D: The object is in a valid but unspecified state; using it without reassignment is a logic bug.

Question: In C++, a `std::vector<bool>` is returned and you take a reference to an element. Why is this type a famous trap?
Option A: bool cannot live in a vector.
Option B: vector<bool> is faster and always the right default.
Option C: It is the only vector that does not reallocate.
Option D: vector<bool> is a bit-packed proxy; references/pointers to elements are not real bool&.

Question: In C++, a function takes `const std::string&` and you store that reference on an object that outlives the call. A caller passed a string literal. What happens?
Option A: const references extend any temporary to the lifetime of the storing object.
Option B: The compiler is required to reject storing a reference to a parameter.
Option C: The literal lives for the program lifetime, so the stored reference is always safe.
Option D: The temporary std::string dies at the end of the full expression; the stored reference dangles. Own a std::string, or do not store views/references to arguments.

Question: In C++, members are listed `A a; B b;` but the initializer list is `b(...), a(b.x)`. What is the bug?
Option A: C++ sorts the initializer list to be safe.
Option B: You cannot mention other members in an initializer list at all.
Option C: Initializer-list order is the run order, so b is constructed first.
Option D: Members construct in declaration order, not list order; a is initialized first, using a not-yet-constructed b. That is undefined behavior.

Question: In C++, when should you prefer `unique_ptr` over `shared_ptr`?
Option A: shared_ptr is always lock-free and therefore faster.
Option B: Always use shared_ptr; unique_ptr cannot be returned from functions.
Option C: When one owner is enough: unique_ptr is cheaper (no control block/atomics) and makes ownership obvious.
Option D: unique_ptr cannot hold arrays, so shared_ptr is required for buffers.

Question: In C++, why is RAII (owning a resource in an object whose destructor releases it) the default answer to leaks and lock-forget bugs?
Option A: RAII disables exceptions, so you cannot forget a catch.
Option B: new/delete become undefined if any class has a destructor.
Option C: Destructors run on every control-flow exit from the scope, including exceptions, so release is tied to lifetime.
Option D: The compiler inserts garbage collection for RAII types.

Question: In C++, why is `std::string_view` pointing at a temporary `std::string` a dangling-view bug?
Option A: string_view does not own the buffer; when the temporary dies the view is invalid.
Option B: Temporaries live until the process exits.
Option C: string_view is illegal on temporaries and will not compile.
Option D: string_view copies the characters, so it cannot dangle.

Question: In C++, you `new` an object and `delete` it in some return paths but not after an early `return` on error. What is the RAII alternative?
Option A: Wrap the pointer in unique_ptr so the destructor deletes on every exit path.
Option B: Add more comments on the delete.
Option C: Use a raw pointer and a finally keyword.
Option D: Disable exceptions so early returns cannot happen.

Question: In C++, you `push_back` 10 million times on a vector with no reserve, then keep pointers to earlier elements. What are the two problems?
Option A: vector is a linked structure, so pointers stay valid and growth is free.
Option B: The compiler forbids holding pointers while push_back is used.
Option C: push_back is O(1) worst-case and pointers into a vector never dangle.
Option D: Repeated realloc copies the buffer (and can be quadratic if growth is naive), and reallocation invalidates pointers/iterators into the old storage.

Question: In C++, you compile without `-Wall` and ignore a `return` missing on one path. What class of bug is that?
Option A: Undefined behavior: falling off a non-void function.
Option B: The compiler inserts throw.
Option C: C++ requires all paths to return, so this cannot compile.
Option D: A style issue with defined behavior (returns 0).

Question: In C++, you define a destructor that frees a raw pointer but leave copy/move defaulted. What happens on copy?
Option A: Destructors disable copying at compile time always.
Option B: The compiler deletes copies because you wrote a destructor.
Option C: Default copy duplicates the pointer; both destructors free it (double-free). If you write one of the five, define or delete the rest — or use unique_ptr and the rule of zero.
Option D: Default copy deep-clones malloc memory.

Question: In C++, you include a using-directive `using namespace std;` in a header. Why is that a problem?
Option A: std cannot be used in headers.
Option B: Every translation unit that includes it gets std dumped into the global namespace, causing name clashes.
Option C: It disables ADL.
Option D: Headers cannot have using-declarations of any kind.

Question: In C++, you store pointers to vector elements, then `push_back` until capacity grows. What happened?
Option A: vector is a linked structure, so pointers always stay valid.
Option B: push_back is illegal while pointers exist; it will not compile.
Option C: Pointers remain valid because vector is contiguous.
Option D: Reallocation invalidates pointers/iterators into the old buffer (undefined behavior if you use them).

Question: In Cassandra, LWTs (lightweight transactions / IF clauses) are expensive mainly because they…
Option A: Run a Paxos-style round of agreement instead of a regular quorum write
Option B: Store extra bloom filters
Option C: Disable compaction
Option D: Skip the commit log

Question: In Cassandra, RF=3 and you write with CL=ONE. A client then reads with CL=ONE from a different replica. What can happen?
Option A: The read is guaranteed to see the write because ONE always hits the leader.
Option B: The read may miss the write: ONE only waits for one replica, which might not be the one that stored the write yet.
Option C: Cassandra will block the read until all replicas have the write.
Option D: CL=ONE automatically upgrades to QUORUM for the next read.

Question: In Cassandra, if RF=3 and you choose CL=ALL, what availability tradeoff did you make?
Option A: Writes become local-only
Option B: Hints are no longer stored
Option C: You can tolerate one replica down
Option D: Any one replica down makes the request fail, in exchange for seeing all copies

Question: In Cassandra, replication factor (RF) vs consistency level (CL): which statement is accurate?
Option A: RF only applies to reads; CL only applies to writes
Option B: RF is how many replicas store a partition; CL is how many replicas must respond for this read or write
Option C: They are the same setting with two names
Option D: CL decides where data is stored; RF decides how many acknowledgements you wait for

Question: In Cassandra, the coordinator node in a write path is responsible for…
Option A: Storing the only copy of the data
Option B: Sending the mutation to the replica set and waiting for CL acknowledgements
Option C: Choosing a new partition key
Option D: Running repair before every write

Question: In Cassandra, what do clustering columns control?
Option A: Sort order of rows within a partition on disk and in queries
Option B: The replication factor
Option C: Whether hinted handoff is enabled
Option D: Which datacenter gets the write

Question: In Cassandra, what does repair (anti-entropy) try to fix?
Option A: Replicas that have diverged because of missed writes, downtime, or missed hints
Option B: The need for a partition key
Option C: Tombstone creation
Option D: Hot partitions by splitting tokens automatically

Question: In Cassandra, what is hinted handoff for?
Option A: Speeding up range scans
Option B: The coordinator stores a hint when a replica is down, then replays it when the replica returns
Option C: Choosing the partition key
Option D: Replacing anti-entropy repair entirely

Question: In Cassandra, why is a full-table scan (ALLOW FILTERING / unbounded partition scan) a junior anti-pattern?
Option A: Cassandra cannot read more than one row
Option B: Data is partitioned by token; a cluster-wide scan fans out and can overwhelm many nodes
Option C: QUORUM forbids scans
Option D: Tombstones cannot be read

Question: In Cassandra, why should a partition not grow without bound (wide partition)?
Option A: Clustering order breaks after a few rows
Option B: Compaction, repair, caching, and reads of that partition concentrate work on one token and huge SSTable pieces
Option C: RF becomes 1 automatically
Option D: QUORUM cannot count replicas for wide partitions

Question: In Cassandra, with RF=3, what does a QUORUM write mean?
Option A: Exactly 1 replica must acknowledge
Option B: All 3 replicas must acknowledge
Option C: At least 2 replicas must acknowledge (majority of RF)
Option D: Only the coordinator stores the write

Question: In Cassandra, you need to fetch a user's last 100 events in time order. How should that be modeled?
Option A: Partition key = event id, so every event is its own partition for even load.
Option B: Partition key = user id, clustering key = event time, so one partition holds an ordered slice you can range-read.
Option C: A single partition for the whole table named `events` so ORDER BY always works globally.
Option D: Store events in a Cassandra collection column and let CQL sort them at query time across nodes.

Question: In Cassandra, you write at CL=ONE and later read at CL=ONE. Why might you miss your own write?
Option A: ONE always waits for all replicas
Option B: Tombstones block all reads at ONE
Option C: Cassandra never reads your own writes
Option D: The read may hit a replica that has not received the write yet

Question: What does the partition key actually control in Cassandra?
Option A: The consistency level of the query
Option B: Whether a bloom filter is used
Option C: The on-disk sort order of rows inside a partition
Option D: Which node(s) own the data: it hashes to a token and thus a replica set

Question: What is a tombstone in Cassandra?
Option A: A repair session identifier
Option B: A backup of a deleted SSTable
Option C: A deletion marker that must be stored and compacted away later so old values do not resurrect
Option D: A hint stored on a coordinator

Question: Why can a hot partition ruin a Cassandra cluster even when total QPS looks modest?
Option A: Cassandra cannot store large partitions
Option B: QUORUM is disabled for hot keys
Option C: Bloom filters stop working on busy nodes
Option D: One token/partition is owned by a small replica set, so those nodes take all the load for that key

Question: Why is DELETE in Cassandra not the same as 'the row is gone now'?
Option A: Deletes require a QUORUM of all clusters worldwide.
Option B: Deletes are stored as tombstones and kept until gc_grace so repair does not resurrect the row.
Option C: Cassandra cannot delete; you can only TTL the whole table.
Option D: DELETE drops the SSTable file immediately, which is why deletes are fast.

Question: In data structures and algorithms, DFS vs BFS for 'does a path exist in a huge, deep, narrow maze if you are memory-constrained'?
Option A: DFS uses stack proportional to depth, which can be smaller than BFS's frontier in a wide graph — but it can also go infinitely deep without extra guards
Option B: BFS always uses less memory than DFS
Option C: They use identical memory on every graph
Option D: Only union-find can test connectivity

Question: In data structures and algorithms, a Bloom filter says 'this user id is not in the set.' What can you conclude?
Option A: You must re-hash with a tree to confirm negatives
Option B: The filter is corrupted whenever it says no
Option C: It is definitely not in the set — Bloom filters have false positives, not false negatives (for a static membership filter)
Option D: It might still be in the set; negatives are probabilistic

Question: In data structures and algorithms, a Bloom filter says 'yes, this email was seen.' You skip sending. Risk?
Option A: LRU will convert the maybe into a no
Option B: False positive — you may skip a never-seen email; if skips are costly, store a real set or a cache in front of source of truth
Option C: False negative — Bloom filters invent missing emails
Option D: Union-find will correct it on the next hop

Question: In data structures and algorithms, a Bloom filter says a user id is 'not present'. How should you treat that?
Option A: Trust it: Bloom filters have false positives, not false negatives (for the items actually inserted).
Option B: It is a cache, so 'not present' means 'evicted', not 'absent'.
Option C: Bloom filters only work for strings, not ids.
Option D: It might be a false negative; check the database anyway.

Question: In data structures and algorithms, an LRU cache is hit on every request for a hot key. What must the structure do in O(1) expected time?
Option A: BFS the keyspace
Option B: Hash map to the node plus a recency list (or equivalent) so lookup, move-to-front, and eviction of the tail are cheap
Option C: Scan the whole array to find the oldest timestamp
Option D: Rebuild a heap from scratch on every hit

Question: In data structures and algorithms, consistent hashing places both keys and nodes on a ring. A node dies. What should happen to its keys?
Option A: A Bloom filter deletes the node
Option B: LRU evicts all keys cluster-wide
Option C: They move to the next node(s) on the ring (or to replicas), not to a random reshuffle of the whole keyspace
Option D: Every key is rehashed with % (N-1)

Question: In data structures and algorithms, why do textbook linked-list queues often lose to a ring buffer of the same logical operations on real hardware?
Option A: CPUs cannot follow pointers at all
Option B: The kernel refuses to allocate list nodes
Option C: Each node is a separate allocation; pointer chasing misses cache and TLB, while a contiguous buffer hits cache lines and prefetches
Option D: Linked lists have worse big-O for enqueue than arrays in the RAM model

Question: In data structures and algorithms, why is a linked list usually the wrong 'insert in the middle is O(1)' answer on real hardware?
Option A: CPUs execute linked-list code in O(n^2) regardless of length.
Option B: Pointer chasing destroys cache locality; an array/vector often wins even if Big-O looks worse.
Option C: Linked lists cannot insert in the middle.
Option D: The OS forbids heap-allocated nodes in user space.

Question: In data structures and algorithms, you add a cache node and want existing keys to mostly stay put. Why not hash(key) % N?
Option A: Heaps cannot store the modulus
Option B: Changing N remaps almost every key; consistent hashing (or Rendezvous) moves only a ~1/N fraction
Option C: Modulo is cryptographically unsafe, so caches reject it
Option D: % N cannot be computed for strings

Question: In data structures and algorithms, you have n chat rooms and union operations 'merge these two rooms' plus 'are these users in the same room?' Which structure?
Option A: Union-find (disjoint-set) with path compression / union by rank
Option B: A max-heap of room ids
Option C: BFS from user 0 on every query
Option D: A Bloom filter of pairs

Question: In data structures and algorithms, you iterate a large array of structs vs a linked list of the same structs, summing one field. Why is the array usually much faster?
Option A: The compiler forbids summing list nodes
Option B: Sequential access prefetches; the list jumps to heap allocations that evict useful cache lines
Option C: Arrays have better big-O for a linear scan than lists
Option D: Linked lists cannot store structs

Question: In data structures and algorithms, you need 'get user by id' at huge QPS, ids are arbitrary strings, no range queries. Which shape fits the workload?
Option A: DFS forest, because ids form a graph
Option B: Hash table (average O(1) point lookup) — a tree adds comparison overhead you do not need, a heap is not a dictionary
Option C: Binary heap, because it always stores the minimum id on top
Option D: Linked list, because pointers are faster than arrays

Question: In data structures and algorithms, you need O(1) expected lookup by id and do not need ordered iteration. What is the default structure, and when does it bite you?
Option A: Hash table: great until a bad hash, huge load factor, or you need range queries / sorted order.
Option B: Linked list: lookups are O(1) with a head pointer.
Option C: Heap: find-min is O(1), so find-by-id is too.
Option D: Balanced BST: lookups are O(1).

Question: In data structures and algorithms, you need the next job with the highest priority, repeatedly, while jobs arrive. Hash, tree, or heap?
Option A: Heap (priority queue) — extract-max/min is the operation; a hash has no order, an ordered tree can do it but with more overhead if you only need the extreme
Option B: Hash table keyed by priority, because priorities are unique
Option C: Singly linked list scanned from the head only
Option D: Bloom filter of finished jobs

Question: In data structures and algorithms, you need the shortest number of hops in an unweighted graph (site crawler, maze). BFS or DFS?
Option A: A heap of random nodes
Option B: BFS — the first time you reach a node is a minimum-hop path; DFS can dive down a long dead end first
Option C: DFS — recursion always yields shortest paths
Option D: Either, because both visit the same nodes

Question: In data structures and algorithms, you sort a list of (name, score) by score descending with an unstable sort, then by name. What breaks?
Option A: Unstable sorts cannot compare integers
Option B: Heaps cannot sort pairs
Option C: BFS will restore the score order
Option D: People with the same name no longer keep score order from the first pass — the second key scramble depends on stability of the name sort

Question: In data structures and algorithms, you sort invoices by date, then by customer, and you need all of one customer's invoices to stay in date order. What property do you need from the second sort?
Option A: Stability — equal keys (same customer) keep their previous (date) order
Option B: In-place partitioning
Option C: That the sort is a heap sort, which is always stable
Option D: Bloom-filter uniqueness of dates

Question: In DynamoDB, a dashboard needs every order from last year with no known user or order id. Why is a table Scan usually the wrong first design?
Option A: Scan is strongly consistent and therefore forbidden
Option B: Scan cannot paginate
Option C: Scan can only return one item
Option D: Scan walks the whole table, burns read capacity on irrelevant items, and gets slower as data grows

Question: In DynamoDB, a product table uses status as the partition key, and almost every item is ACTIVE. Writes start throttling even though table-level capacity looks unused. What is the real problem?
Option A: Sort keys are required for every write
Option B: DynamoDB cannot store more than one item per partition key
Option C: A low-cardinality partition key funnels traffic onto too few partitions (hot keys)
Option D: On-demand mode ignores partition keys

Question: In DynamoDB, a single celebrity userId receives a huge fraction of likes. Adaptive capacity cannot fully save you because:
Option A: On-demand tables do not shard
Option B: GSIs ignore partition keys
Option C: All items for one partition key still share that key's throughput ceiling
Option D: DynamoDB forbids popular keys

Question: In DynamoDB, a table has a sharp weekday peak and near-zero nights. What capacity shape fits without overpaying all week?
Option A: Provisioned at the peak 24/7
Option B: On-demand, or provisioned with auto scaling that tracks the daily curve
Option C: A global table in every region
Option D: A Scan instead of Query

Question: In DynamoDB, a table's partition key is `status` with values OPEN/CLOSED, and almost all traffic is OPEN. What goes wrong as you scale?
Option A: Global secondary indexes automatically rebalance the key, so nothing happens.
Option B: DynamoDB converts the table to a scan-optimized layout and latency improves.
Option C: DynamoDB will reject the table because partition keys must be UUIDs.
Option D: Most requests hash to the same partition (a hot key), so that shard throttles while others sit idle.

Question: In DynamoDB, eventually consistent reads are the default because they:
Option A: Cost less and are enough when the client can tolerate a brief lag after a write
Option B: Bypass partition limits
Option C: Are the only option for GetItem
Option D: Always return stale data

Question: In DynamoDB, filter expressions on a Scan or Query run after capacity is consumed. What does that imply?
Option A: Filters are a substitute for a good key design
Option B: You still pay to read items that the filter later throws away
Option C: Filters make the operation strongly consistent
Option D: Filters avoid partition throttling

Question: In DynamoDB, high partition-key cardinality matters because:
Option A: DynamoDB only allows 10 distinct keys
Option B: Many distinct, relatively even keys let the service spread load; a handful of keys cannot
Option C: Cardinality enables strongly consistent GSIs
Option D: Cardinality removes the 400KB limit

Question: In DynamoDB, on-demand vs provisioned capacity is mainly a statement about workload shape. Which pairing is right?
Option A: On-demand only for strongly consistent reads
Option B: Provisioned only for tables without sort keys
Option C: On-demand removes partition-key hotspots
Option D: On-demand for spiky or unknown traffic; provisioned for steady, forecastable load

Question: In DynamoDB, what does a well-chosen partition key actually control?
Option A: Whether reads are strongly consistent
Option B: The maximum item size
Option C: Which AWS region stores the table
Option D: How traffic is spread across storage partitions

Question: In DynamoDB, what is the practical difference between GetItem and Query?
Option A: They are identical if eventual consistency is on
Option B: GetItem needs the full primary key for one item; Query reads a partition (optionally a sort-key range)
Option C: Query cannot use a sort key
Option D: GetItem always scans the table

Question: In DynamoDB, when should you choose a strongly consistent read over the default eventually consistent read?
Option A: Whenever you want cheaper reads
Option B: When the next decision cannot tolerate a replica that has not yet seen the latest write to that item
Option C: When reading from a global secondary index
Option D: When the item is larger than 400KB

Question: In DynamoDB, why do engineers treat the 400KB item size cap as a modeling constraint, not just a storage limit?
Option A: Secondary indexes cannot project attributes under 400KB

Option C: Larger items must be split across partitions automatically
Option D: Every read and write moves the whole item, so fat items amplify latency, cost, and hot-partition risk

Question: In DynamoDB, why is Scan the wrong default for a user-facing request path?
Option A: Scan reads every partition; cost and latency grow with table size instead of with the result you need.
Option B: Scan is eventually consistent only and cannot be strongly consistent.
Option C: Scan is disabled once a table has a sort key.

Question: In DynamoDB, you know userId and want that user's orders in a time range. Which operation matches the data model?
Option A: BatchWriteItem to read

Question: Why store a profile photo URL (or S3 key) in DynamoDB instead of the image bytes?
Option A: URLs are the only string type DynamoDB allows

Option C: S3 cannot store images

Question: You need all orders for a customer in date order. Which key design matches how DynamoDB actually partitions data?

Question: In generative AI, RAG still fails when:

Question: In Java, `List<String> xs = Arrays.asList("a", "b"); xs.add("c");` What goes wrong?

Question: In Java, a JPA entity implements equals on a database id that is null until persist. You put two new entities in a HashSet before save. What happens?

Question: In Java, a REST handler does `catch (Exception e) { }` and returns 200. What did you just hide?
Option A: Empty catch blocks are stripped by the compiler in production.

Question: In Java, a hot path does `list.get(i)` on a million-element list. A teammate switches ArrayList to LinkedList 'because inserts in the middle are O(1)'. What happens?

Question: In Java, two threads do `volatile int n; n++;` to count requests. Why is this still wrong?

Option D: Callers can lock on the same instance and deadlock with you; you leaked the lock identity.

Question: In Java, you build a 50,000-line report with `s = s + line + "\n"` in a loop. Why does this explode in time and garbage?

Question: In Java, you use a record `Point(int x, int y)` as a HashMap key. A teammate adds a mutable `List<Tag> tags` component. Why is that a trap?

Question: In Java, you write `int n = scores.get(userId);` where scores is `Map<String, Integer>`. The id is missing. What happens, and why?

Question: In Kubernetes, a PodDisruptionBudget with minAvailable: 2 on a 3-replica app is mainly protecting you from what?

Question: In Kubernetes, a pod has no memory request/limit. A noisy neighbor on the node allocates RAM. What is the most typical outcome for your pod?

Question: In Kubernetes, a pod is serving traffic correctly, but you wire the liveness probe to the same database health check as readiness. The database blips for 10 seconds. What happens?

Question: In Kubernetes, a pod that needs disk should reference a PVC, not a raw disk path. Why?

Question: In Kubernetes, a rolling update is stuck: new pods are not Ready, old pods are still serving. Which knob is doing its job?

Option C: :latest tags cannot roll forward, only backward

Question: In Kubernetes, readiness probe is failing, liveness is passing. User impact?

Question: A secondary index in InnoDB does not store the row. How are remaining columns fetched?

Option D: To the replica: replicas are always transactionally caught up if you use InnoDB.

Question: In MySQL, a replica shows Seconds_Behind_Source growing during a long transaction on the source. Why can lag jump at COMMIT rather than during the transaction?
Option A: Binlog events for the transaction are dumped as a unit at commit, so the replica applier sees a burst only then
Option B: InnoDB on the source does not write undo until COMMIT
Option C: Gap locks are replayed only after the replica VACUUM
Option D: The replica buffer pool is flushed at every source statement

Question: In MySQL, online DDL (INPLACE/INSTANT) still fails or blocks writes for some ALTER types. Which change is least likely to stay fully online?
Option A: Changing a column type in a way that requires a table rebuild and row conversion
Option B: Adding a nullable column with INSTANT metadata-only support on a compatible version
Option C: Adding a secondary index with INPLACE
Option D: Dropping a secondary index

Question: In MySQL, statement-based binlog vs row-based. A statement uses UUID() or a non-deterministic UDF. What is the replica risk with SBR?
Option A: The replica executes the statement again and can produce different row values than the source
Option B: Row-based logging cannot replicate UPDATEs
Option C: Gap locks are not written to the binlog
Option D: The buffer pool is not updated on the replica

Question: In MySQL, why is a covering secondary index often faster than one that only has the filter columns?
Option A: Covering indexes disable the buffer pool, so they skip RAM and read SSD sequentially.
Option B: MySQL can then use statement-based replication for that query.
Option C: Covering indexes are stored in the query cache instead of InnoDB.
Option D: It avoids the extra clustered-index lookup to fetch remaining selected columns.

Question: In MySQL, you add an index to fix a slow WHERE, but writes to that table drop in throughput. What is the direct cause?
Option A: Covering indexes disable the buffer pool
Option B: Online DDL remains running in the background forever
Option C: Every INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE must maintain another btree, with extra undo, redo, and change-buffer or page-split work
Option D: InnoDB allows only one secondary index per table at runtime

Question: In MySQL, you run SELECT ... FOR UPDATE WHERE id < 100 on a sparse PK. Why can concurrent inserts of id=50 block even if 50 did not exist?
Option A: The binary log must serialize all inserts under RR
Option B: Gap locks cover the gaps between existing records in the scanned range
Option C: InnoDB locks the entire table for any range WHERE
Option D: UUID primary keys disable row locks

Question: In MySQL, you run `SELECT ... FOR UPDATE` on a range in REPEATABLE READ. Why can that block inserts into gaps you did not think you locked?
Option A: Gap locks are a MyISAM feature and InnoDB ignores them.
Option B: InnoDB next-key / gap locks exist to prevent phantoms, so they lock index records and the gaps between them.
Option C: MySQL converts every range lock into a table lock in REPEATABLE READ.
Option D: FOR UPDATE only locks the rows that already exist; inserts are blocked by the binary log.

Question: InnoDB stores the clustered index as the table. Why is a random UUID primary key often a scaling problem?
Option A: Inserts scatter across leaf pages, causing page splits, fragmentation, and poor buffer-pool locality
Option B: UUID values cannot be indexed in InnoDB
Option C: Secondary indexes cannot point at a UUID clustered key
Option D: Gap locks are disabled when the PK is not numeric

Question: InnoDB stores the full row in the primary-key B-tree. What does that imply for a secondary index lookup?
Option A: The secondary index stores the primary key; InnoDB then looks up the clustered index to get the row.
Option B: Secondary indexes always require a table scan of the .ibd file.
Option C: Secondary indexes cannot be used if the primary key is a composite.
Option D: The secondary index contains the full row too, so one lookup is enough.

Question: READ COMMITTED in InnoDB uses fewer gap locks than REPEATABLE READ for many statements. What trade-off do you accept?
Option A: The clustered index is no longer used
Option B: Each statement sees a new snapshot, so non-repeatable reads and some write skew patterns become possible
Option C: Dirty reads of uncommitted data become allowed
Option D: The binary log can only be STATEMENT

Question: REPEATABLE READ in InnoDB uses next-key (record + gap) locks for many UPDATE/SELECT ... FOR UPDATE scans. What anomaly is this trying to prevent?
Option A: Replica lag on statement-based binlog
Option B: Phantoms: another transaction inserting a row into the scanned range
Option C: Dirty reads of uncommitted data from other transactions
Option D: Loss of the clustered index after COMMIT

Question: The InnoDB buffer pool is smaller than the working set of clustered + secondary indexes. What is the first performance failure?
Option A: Page misses cause read I/O on both index trees, and eviction of dirty pages adds write I/O
Option B: InnoDB falls back to MyISAM for those tables
Option C: Gap locks are released immediately to save memory
Option D: The binary log is disabled automatically

Question: Under InnoDB REPEATABLE READ, a consistent snapshot SELECT (no FOR UPDATE) can still miss rows inserted and committed by others after your snapshot. That is expected MVCC. When do people still get surprised by phantoms?
Option A: When row-based binlog is enabled
Option B: When they mix snapshot reads with locking reads, or assume RR plus locks behaves like SERIALIZABLE for all statements
Option C: When the buffer pool is fully warmed
Option D: When the primary key is sequential

Question: Why does a wide PRIMARY KEY make every secondary index larger in InnoDB?
Option A: InnoDB compresses only the primary key
Option B: Gap locks require the PK to be stored twice
Option C: Each secondary leaf stores the full clustered key as the row locator
Option D: Secondary indexes duplicate every column of the table

Question: A long-running analytics query is reading a table while OLTP traffic keeps updating it. Why don't those writers typically block the analytics reader in PostgreSQL?
Option A: Readers see a snapshot of row versions; writers create new versions instead of overwriting the row the reader is using.
Option B: PostgreSQL copies the whole table to a temp file for every SELECT, so writers cannot touch it.
Option C: Writers take table-level exclusive locks, so the reader is queued in a wait list and then replayed from WAL.
Option D: Each writer updates in place; the reader always sees the latest bytes and never needs old versions.

Question: Connection pooling is added in front of PostgreSQL because each backend is a process. Which pooling mistake still exhausts the server?
Option A: Opening a new server connection per client request and holding idle transactions open
Option B: Using transaction pooling for sessions that never SET session state
Option C: Capping pool size below max_connections
Option D: Routing read-only queries to a hot standby

Question: In PostgreSQL, EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS) shows a Nested Loop with huge actual rows vs estimated rows. What is the most likely operational risk?
Option A: The inner scan is executed far more times than planned, exploding I/O and runtime
Option B: WAL volume drops because nested loops skip checkpoints
Option C: VACUUM cannot run while Nested Loop is chosen
Option D: synchronous_commit is forced off for the query

Question: In PostgreSQL, HOT (Heap-Only Tuple) updates skip index maintenance. Which condition prevents HOT and causes extra index churn?
Option A: The UPDATE changes a column that is part of an index, so a new index entry is required
Option B: The table has no indexes at all
Option C: fillfactor is 100 and there is free space on the page
Option D: The transaction isolation level is READ COMMITTED

Question: In PostgreSQL, READ COMMITTED vs REPEATABLE READ: a counter is incremented by two concurrent transactions. Which isolation surprise is unique to READ COMMITTED?
Option A: Indexes are locked in SHARE mode for the whole transaction
Option B: Each statement can see rows committed after the transaction started, so two increments can both succeed on different versions
Option C: Dead tuples cannot be vacuumed until both transactions end
Option D: WAL is written twice for the same tuple

Question: In PostgreSQL, VACUUM exists primarily because of which MVCC side effect?
Option A: Dead row versions and leftover transaction IDs accumulate; something must reclaim that space and freeze XIDs.
Option B: WAL cannot be archived until VACUUM copies it to the heap.
Option C: Foreign keys are not checked until VACUUM runs.
Option D: Indexes forget about committed rows until VACUUM rebuilds them from scratch.

Question: In PostgreSQL, a btree index on a low-cardinality status column is used for WHERE status = 'active' on a table that is 90% active. Why can this index hurt?
Option A: Btree cannot store boolean-like values
Option B: MVCC visibility is checked only in indexes, never the heap
Option C: Autovacuum refuses to analyze indexed columns
Option D: The index points at most heap pages, adding random I/O on top of reading nearly the whole table

Question: In PostgreSQL, a buggy ORM issues a join that never finishes. You want the database to kill it before it holds locks and fills work_mem. Which timeout is the right first lever, and what does it not cover?
Option A: PostgreSQL has no query timeout; you must kill backends from the OS
Option B: statement_timeout aborts that SQL; it does not cancel a session that is idle-in-transaction after the statement ended — that needs idle_in_transaction_session_timeout (and lock_timeout for waiters)
Option C: lock_timeout kills running queries even if they hold no locks
Option D: statement_timeout also rolls back idle-in-transaction sessions automatically

Question: In PostgreSQL, a client holds a session-level SET and a WITH HOLD cursor, then you switch the pooler to transaction pooling. What breaks?
Option A: VACUUM FULL runs after every COMMIT
Option B: Session state and held cursors are not bound to a single backend across transactions
Option C: WAL shipping to replicas stops
Option D: MVCC snapshots become SERIALIZABLE automatically

Question: In PostgreSQL, a long-running report transaction sits idle in the same database as a busy OLTP table. Why can autovacuum fail to reclaim dead tuples on that table even after many updates?
Option A: PostgreSQL never vacuums a table that still has indexes
Option B: Dead tuples are only stored in WAL and never in heap pages
Option C: Idle transactions automatically freeze all XIDs so vacuum has nothing to do
Option D: VACUUM still runs, but it cannot remove tuples still visible to that session's snapshot, so dead rows accumulate until the snapshot ends

Question: In PostgreSQL, a query plan shows Seq Scan on a 50-row lookup table that has a btree index on the filter column. When is the sequential scan often the better choice?
Option A: When the index is unique, sequential scan is always preferred
Option B: When work_mem is large, indexes are ignored
Option C: When the column is NOT NULL, btree indexes cannot be used
Option D: When most of the table will be visited anyway, random index I/O costs more than reading the heap once

Question: In PostgreSQL, after an UPDATE that does not change any indexed column, you still see a new heap tuple. What MVCC behavior explains this?
Option A: Indexes store full row copies, so the heap is rewritten only for uniqueness checks
Option B: MVCC reuses the same tuple slot in place and never creates a new version
Option C: Updates are logged only in WAL; the heap is never rewritten until CHECKPOINT
Option D: PostgreSQL always copies the whole row so readers of the old snapshot keep a consistent version

Question: In PostgreSQL, streaming replication with a hot standby is lagging. Which primary-side behavior most directly grows replica apply delay?
Option A: synchronous_commit = on on the standby only

Question: In PostgreSQL, table bloat after heavy UPDATE/DELETE is high, but pg_stat_user_tables.n_dead_tup is low. What can still make the table large on disk?
Option A: TOAST is never vacuumed so it always grows

Question: In PostgreSQL, you added a B-tree index on a boolean `is_deleted` column that is false for 99% of rows. Most queries filter `WHERE is_deleted = false`. What is the most likely result?
Option A: The index will usually beat a sequential scan because booleans are tiny.

Question: In PostgreSQL, you partition a large events table by day. Which query pattern fails to benefit and may get worse?

Option D: Queries that constrain the partition key to a single day

Question: In PostgreSQL, you set synchronous_commit = off for a burst of non-critical inserts. What failure mode did you accept?

Option C: Indexes become invalid because index WAL is not written
Option D: A crash can lose recent committed transactions even though clients already saw COMMIT succeed

Question: Why does PostgreSQL write to WAL before applying the same change to the heap file?
Option A: WAL is only for logical replication and is not used on a single node.

Question: Your app opens a new PostgreSQL connection for every HTTP request and closes it at the end. Under load the database CPU is fine but new requests stall. What is the usual bottleneck?

Question: In Python, `class Cart: items = []` then `Cart().items.append(x)`. Why do carts share items?

Question: In Python, `if user_id:` skips id 0 (or an empty string). Why is that a bug for identifiers?

Option C: The buffer pool allows only one dirty page at a time on replicas
Option D: Transactions that touch overlapping rows or lack writeset information cannot be applied concurrently without violating commit order

Question: In MySQL, row-based replication plus a table without a primary key. Why does replica apply become extremely slow?
Option A: RBR refuses to replicate tables without a PK
Option B: Gap locks cannot be reconstructed without a PK
Option C: The buffer pool disables change buffering on those tables
Option D: Each row event may require a table scan or hidden index lookup to find the row, instead of a clustered PK point lookup

Question: In MySQL, statement-based binlog plus a non-deterministic `UPDATE ... ORDER BY RAND() LIMIT 1` is replicated. What goes wrong?
Option A: Replicas apply the same statement and may update different rows than the primary.
Option B: InnoDB refuses to log non-deterministic statements.
Option C: The statement is rewritten to row-based automatically and cannot diverge.
Option D: RAND() is stored in GTID, so replicas replay the same choice.

Question: In MySQL, you enable semi-sync so a failover replica must ACK before the client is told COMMIT. After a primary crash, the promoted replica can still miss a transaction the client saw as committed. Why?
Option A: Semi-sync writes the binlog only on the replica, so the primary never had the transaction
Option B: InnoDB disables redo on the primary when semi-sync is on, so crash recovery is empty
Option C: GTID makes every ACK'd transaction present on every replica before COMMIT returns
Option D: Semi-sync is not 'the replica you promote flushed the ACK': AFTER_COMMIT can return before the replica durable-fsyncs, and you might promote a different replica than the one that ACK'd

Question: In MySQL, you need to purge millions of rows without stalling the replica. Why is DELETE in small PK batches often preferred over one huge transaction?
Option A: InnoDB cannot DELETE more than 1000 rows in one statement
Option B: Gap locks are only taken on small batches
Option C: Row-based binlog ignores large transactions
Option D: A huge transaction delays binlog dump until commit, holds undo, and creates a massive apply burst; batches bound lag and purge history

Question: In MySQL, you switch binlog_format to ROW to make replicas match. Which source-side cost appears?
Option A: Binlog volume grows because before/after row images are written, especially for wide rows and bulk updates
Option B: InnoDB disables the redo log
Option C: Gap locks are written into the binlog for every SELECT
Option D: Online DDL becomes COPY-only

Question: You chose a random UUID as the InnoDB primary key for a huge table. Why do writes get worse over time?
Option A: Inserts scatter across the clustered index, causing page splits and random I/O instead of appending to the right edge.
Option B: UUID PKs disable the change buffer, so secondary indexes cannot be updated.
Option C: InnoDB stores UUID PKs twice, doubling row size.
Option D: UUIDs cannot be indexed in InnoDB.

Question: innodb_flush_log_at_trx_commit = 2 improves COMMIT latency. What durability did you give up?
Option A: A host crash can lose the last second of committed transactions even though clients saw COMMIT
Option B: Replicas will diverge on every DDL
Option C: Gap locks are not released at COMMIT
Option D: The clustered index can tear pages without redo

Question: In PostgreSQL, EXPLAIN shows Bitmap Heap Scan with Recheck Cond and lossy pages under memory pressure. What happened?
Option A: The index was corrupt and PostgreSQL fell back to sequential scan mid-query
Option B: HOT chains cannot be followed in bitmap scans
Option C: synchronous_commit forced a recheck of WAL before visibility
Option D: The bitmap did not fit in work_mem, so some pages are rechecked row-by-row after a coarse page bitmap

Question: In PostgreSQL, a GIN index on jsonb speeds @> queries but INSERTs and VACUUM become expensive. Why?
Option A: GIN disables MVCC visibility checks
Option B: jsonb cannot be TOASTed when GIN exists
Option C: GIN requires sequential scans for all other predicates
Option D: GIN stores many posting-list entries per row and pending lists must be merged, amplifying WAL and cleanup

Question: In PostgreSQL, a covering index (INCLUDE) is created for a read-heavy query. When does INCLUDE still fail to make an index-only scan effective?
Option A: INCLUDE columns cannot be TOASTed
Option B: Index-only scans require SERIALIZABLE
Option C: INCLUDE disables HOT on the table
Option D: The visibility map is not all-visible, so heap fetches still occur for many tuples

Question: In PostgreSQL, a query that should use an index does a sequential scan after a bulk load. Statistics were not updated. What is the planner missing?
Option A: A lock on pg_index that sequential scans skip.
Option B: The physical location of WAL segments.
Option C: Row counts and value distributions; without ANALYZE it can think the table is tiny or the filter is unselective.
Option D: The OS page cache size, which it stores in pg_class.

Question: In PostgreSQL, a replication slot is left unused after a forgotten subscriber. What operational failure follows?
Option A: Hot updates become sequential scans
Option B: max_connections is reduced to 1
Option C: WAL is retained forever for that slot until disk fills and the primary can no longer write
Option D: Autovacuum freezes all tables immediately

Question: In PostgreSQL, a table is 200 GB, updates hit the same hot rows all day, and autovacuum cannot keep up. Indexes keep growing even though live row count is stable. What is actually accumulating?
Option A: Materialized views of every UPDATE, stored until ANALYZE.
Option B: Logical replication slots created automatically for each UPDATE.
Option C: WAL files that VACUUM is required to delete from pg_xlog.
Option D: Dead tuple versions and index entries pointing at them; HOT can skip index updates only when a new version fits on the same page.

Question: In PostgreSQL, a write-heavy table never gets HOT updates even when indexed columns are unchanged. fillfactor is 100. What is the mechanism?
Option A: HOT requires synchronous_commit = off
Option B: HOT only works on partitioned tables
Option C: HOT is disabled when replication slots exist
Option D: No free space on the same page, so the new version is placed elsewhere and every index must be updated

Question: In PostgreSQL, bloat in a btree index grows even though the heap was recently vacuumed. What index-specific issue remains?
Option A: HOT updates always bloat indexes first
Option B: Indexes are only compacted at xid freeze time
Option C: Index pages are not fully recycled by ordinary vacuum; deleted keys can leave poorly reusable space until REINDEX or vacuuming that can recycle pages
Option D: Btree indexes store heap tuple copies that vacuum never visits

Question: In PostgreSQL, logical replication is lagging. The slot's `restart_lsn` is old and disk is filling with WAL. What happens if you drop the slot to free disk without a plan?
Option A: WAL is copied to S3 automatically when a slot is dropped.
Option B: Dropping a slot is refused until the subscriber is caught up.
Option C: Replicas automatically rebuild from a new base backup with no data loss.
Option D: PostgreSQL can recycle WAL, but that subscriber can no longer catch up from the missing segments and needs a resync.

Question: In PostgreSQL, logical replication of a table with frequent UPDATEs of large rows. Replica apply is CPU-bound. What is a common cause?
Option A: The subscriber runs VACUUM FULL after every message
Option B: Partitioning is required for logical decoding
Option C: Row images in WAL plus replica replay of full-row UPDATEs, especially without replica identity index lookups being cheap
Option D: Logical replication ships only HOT chains, which the replica must rebuild

Question: In PostgreSQL, partition-wise joins are not used between two partitioned tables. What typically blocks them?
Option A: Partition keys and bounds do not line up, so the planner cannot join matching partitions independently
Option B: Both tables use btree indexes
Option C: synchronous_commit is on
Option D: The tables are in the same schema

Question: In PostgreSQL, pgBouncer transaction pooling plus prepared statements on the client. What failure mode appears?
Option A: VACUUM cannot run while PgBouncer is used
Option B: Prepared statements are backend-local, so the next transaction may hit a different server process that does not have them
Option C: WAL is not flushed on COMMIT in transaction pooling
Option D: MVCC snapshots leak across pooled clients

Question: In PostgreSQL, xid wraparound autovacuum is running and blocking DDL. Application writes still succeed but get slower. What is going on?
Option A: Anti-wraparound vacuum must scan tables to freeze, competing for I/O and holding locks that conflict with some DDL
Option B: PostgreSQL pauses WAL until freeze completes
Option C: All indexes are rebuilt during wraparound vacuum
Option D: Hot standbys take exclusive locks on the primary

Question: In PostgreSQL, you add a btree index to accelerate a JOIN, but INSERTs slow more than the SELECT savings. Which cost is easy to miss?
Option A: Every heap insert/update/delete must maintain the index, plus WAL for index pages, plus extra vacuum work
Option B: Indexes disable HOT even when the indexed column is unchanged
Option C: Btree indexes prevent TOAST compression
Option D: The planner cannot use an index together with a sequential scan of another table

Question: In PostgreSQL, you need SERIALIZABLE isolation for a 'create user if missing' race. What extra cost should you expect?
Option A: SSI can abort one of the concurrent transactions with a serialization failure; the app must retry.
Option B: SERIALIZABLE disables WAL to get a consistent snapshot.
Option C: PostgreSQL upgrades the table to ACCESS EXCLUSIVE for the rest of the session.
Option D: No extra cost; SERIALIZABLE is implemented with table locks only.

Question: In PostgreSQL, you need replica lag under a few hundred milliseconds for failover. The workload is bursty WAL. Which trade-off is real with synchronous replication?
Option A: Primary COMMIT waits on replica flush/apply, so a slow or dead replica stalls writes
Option B: Synchronous replicas do not write WAL, so lag cannot exist

Question: In PostgreSQL, you set `synchronous_commit=off` to gain write throughput. What did you actually trade?
Option A: Sequential scans become illegal because hint bits are untrusted.

Option D: After a crash you can lose transactions that returned success but had not yet flushed WAL.

Question: In PostgreSQL, you set synchronous_commit = remote_apply for a reporting replica. Compared with on (local flush), what extra wait is introduced?
Option A: The primary waits only for local fsync, same as default
Option B: The replica must VACUUM before ACK
Option C: Index builds on the primary become non-transactional
Option D: The primary waits until the standby has replayed the WAL, not merely received or flushed it

Question: SERIALIZABLE isolation reports a serialization failure on a read-only transaction. Why is that possible in PostgreSQL SSI?
Option A: The read-only snapshot participated in a dangerous rw-dependency cycle with concurrent writers

Question: A memory profile shows objects that should be dead still alive. Cycles of objects with `__del__` are involved. Why is CPython struggling?

Question: In Python, asyncio task is cancelled while awaiting a non-cancellable third-party SDK. What goes wrong?

Question: In Python, you log `logger.info('user %s', user)` vs f-strings. Why might the `%s` form still be preferred in a hot debug logger?

Question: In Python, you store request_id in a global in an asyncio app. Concurrent requests mix IDs in logs. Why?

Question: Two Python modules import each other at module top-level, and a class is half-initialized. What is the production-safe fix?

Question: A Lua script in Redis is attractive for compare-and-set because:
Option A: Lua runs on all cluster nodes as a distributed transaction
Option B: The script runs atomically on that instance's single thread, so no other command interleaves

Option D: It starts emitting false negatives to compensate

Question: In data structures and algorithms, hot-key workload: 1 key is 40% of QPS. Hash partition across 50 caches. What structure-level fact did you ignore?
Option A: A heap of caches will split the key each extract-min
Option B: Consistent hashing splits a single key across the ring by definition
Option C: Hashing spreads keys, not load — one key still lives on one shard; you need replication, local LRU on every node, or a different split (by session, by request) for that key
Option D: A balanced tree on the same key automatically shards it

Question: In data structures and algorithms, rendezvous hashing vs consistent ring: you want minimal disruption and easy weighted nodes without virtual node explosion. Which idea?
Option A: Always use hash % N with sticky sessions
Option B: Put nodes in a heap and extract-min per key
Option C: DFS the node list until a Bloom filter says yes
Option D: Highest random weight / Rendezvous: score(key, node), pick max — membership change only moves keys that preferred the lost node; weights fold into the score

Question: In data structures and algorithms, union-find with path compression, no union-by-rank, adversarial unions always attaching large to small via the wrong root. Practical issue?
Option A: Trees get tall; even with later compression, a bad sequence plus no rank/size can make individual finds scan long chains before they flatten
Option B: Path compression without rank is undefined
Option C: The structure becomes a heap and extract-min breaks
Option D: Bloom filter bits collide with the parent array

Question: In data structures and algorithms, you external-sort huge files. Runs are written, then merged. Why does 'stable' still matter on disk?
Option A: BFS merge of runs preserves order automatically
Option B: Equal keys from earlier files/runs must keep their input order (e.g. original row id, replica timestamp) or the merge invents a new ordering that downstream consumers did not ask for
Option C: Stability only exists in RAM arrays, not files
Option D: Heaps used in k-way merge are stable by nature for all equal keys

Question: In data structures and algorithms, you need an LRU across a fleet. Local LRU per node + consistent hashing. A key's node jumps; the new node has a cold LRU. Besides miss storm, what invariant broke?
Option A: Consistent hashing copies the doubly linked list to the successor automatically
Option B: A heap of timestamps is globally shared via hashing
Option C: BFS of the ring rebuilds LRU
Option D: Recency is per process — the global working set is not on the ring. Hashing moves identity, not the linked-list order; replicas or session stickiness are how you keep recency

Question: In data structures and algorithms, you need connectivity across a huge undirected graph that mutates. Why might union-find (DSU) be the right first tool, and when does it stop?
Option A: BFS from every node is always faster.
Option B: DSU supports deletions as cheaply as unions.
Option C: Near-constant unions/finds for 'are these connected' if you mostly add edges; deletions, path queries, or need for actual paths need a different structure.
Option D: DSU is only for trees of height 2.

Question: In data structures and algorithms, you replace an array-backed deque with a linked list to get 'true O(1) insert in the middle' for a 1e7-element structure you mostly iterate. Net effect on a modern CPU?
Option A: TLB prefers pointer graphs to contiguous pages
Option B: Middle insert may allocate and patch two pointers, but iteration becomes cache-hostile; if iterates dominate, you slowed the real workload
Option C: Linked lists always dominate arrays once n > 10^4
Option D: The allocator colocates list nodes so they prefetch like arrays

Question: In data structures and algorithms, you sort events by (user_id, event_time) for per-user sessionization. One-pass composite compare vs sort-by-time then stable sort-by-user. When is the two-pass actually what you want?
Option A: Two-pass is always slower and never justified
Option B: Heaps can only do one key
Option C: BFS requires two-pass sorts
Option D: When event_time order among a user must be the original sort's order and that first sort was already done (or is expensive to redo as a composite) — stability composes existing order; a new unstable composite can still break equal (user, time) ties you cared about

Question: A cache in front of DynamoDB for a hot product key helps reads. What must you still design for?
Option A: GSIs become strongly consistent
Option B: The cache makes writes strongly consistent across regions
Option C: Cache misses, TTL expiry, and stampede can slam the same hot key; writes still hit DynamoDB
Option D: Partition keys are no longer needed

Question: A product wants relational joins across three DynamoDB tables on the request path. What should you push back with?
Option A: Access-pattern-first: denormalize/duplicate, or pick a database that joins. Request-path joins are N queries, inconsistent snapshots, and hot GSIs waiting to happen.
Option B: Transactions across three tables are free if items are small.
Option C: PartiQL joins are as cheap as Dynamo Query.
Option D: Use Scan + in-memory join; DynamoDB is fine.

Question: Default DynamoDB global tables (MREC) give you multi-region copies. What do they not give you unless you opt into MRSC?
Option A: The same partition-key model in each region
Option B: Lower read latency near a replica
Option C: A single globally strongly consistent item view on every replica — that is a separate, higher-latency MRSC mode, not the default async replica
Option D: Regional isolation if you design for it

Question: In DynamoDB, a 350KB item is updated 20 times a second to flip one flag. Why is this an incident waiting to happen?
Option A: Updates are eventually consistent only
Option B: On-demand forbids updates
Option C: Flags cannot live in DynamoDB
Option D: Each update rewrites the whole large item, multiplying write cost and making that key hotter than the business change requires

Question: In DynamoDB, a GSI is KEYS_ONLY. A query against it still needs five large attributes. Tradeoff?
Option A: You do a cheap index Query then GetItem the base rows; you avoided write amplification at the cost of extra reads
Option B: KEYS_ONLY implies strong consistency
Option C: You must Scan the base table
Option D: The GSI returns those attributes for free

Question: In DynamoDB, a leaderboard GSI partition key is the constant LEADERBOARD. Why will this fail at scale?
Option A: Every write lands on one index partition; you modeled a global hot key
Option B: GSIs cannot sort
Option C: Leaderboards require strongly consistent scans
Option D: Constants are not valid attribute names

Question: In DynamoDB, adaptive capacity moved extra throughput toward a hot partition, but p99 still collapses on one productId. What is left?
Option A: Enable strongly consistent GSIs
Option B: Switch every read to Scan
Option C: Buy more table-level RCUs only
Option D: Change the key (shard, invert access pattern, or cache) because one key is a physical bottleneck

Question: In DynamoDB, exporting to S3 / using an incremental export for analytics is preferred over a live Scan because:
Option A: Scans cannot paginate
Option B: S3 is a database
Option C: You isolate heavy read traffic from the online table's partitions and capacity
Option D: Exports are strongly consistent GSIs

Question: In DynamoDB, on-demand still throttles a partition. Why are people surprised?
Option A: On-demand disables GSIs
Option B: On-demand is only for Scans
Option C: On-demand advertises infinite per-key QPS
Option D: On-demand removes table-level provisioning, not the physics of a single hot key or a sudden jump beyond what that partition can absorb

Question: In DynamoDB, single-table design is not 'put everything in one table'. The actual rule is:
Option A: Minimize the number of AWS resources on the bill
Option B: Shape items and keys so each access pattern is a Query on a partition, not a Scan across entity types
Option C: Never use GSIs
Option D: Store blobs inline to avoid joins

Question: In DynamoDB, streams + Lambda to maintain a projection. The Lambda is not idempotent. What operational failure is guaranteed eventually?
Option A: At-least-once shard records will double-apply; the projection must be idempotent or versioned.
Option B: Lambda retries are disabled for DynamoDB streams.
Option C: Projections cannot diverge because they share storage with the table.
Option D: Streams are exactly-once, so the projection stays correct.

Question: In DynamoDB, strongly consistent reads cost more and still do not make a GSI or a default global-table replica 'the truth everywhere'. The honest contract is:
Option A: Strong reads lock all GSIs
Option B: Strong reads are free on on-demand
Option C: Strong reads disable throttling
Option D: A strong GetItem is a read of that region's partition leader, not a global lock; GSIs stay eventually consistent, and default (MREC) global tables are async unless you chose MRSC

Question: In DynamoDB, time-series data with PK = today's date concentrates today's writes. A better key shape is:
Option A: Shard by a high-cardinality id (device, customer, or time bucket + shard) so ingests spread, and query by the access pattern you actually have
Option B: PK = status ACTIVE
Option C: No partition key, sort key only

Question: In DynamoDB, why model 1:N as partition key = parent and sort key = child rather than embedding an unbounded list on the parent?

Question: In DynamoDB, you are asked to 'just add an index' for an unplanned access pattern. What do you check first?

Option C: Whether items exceed 400KB after indexing

Question: In DynamoDB, you are designing for a 10× Prime-Day-like spike on a few product keys. Adaptive capacity and on-demand help, but what still requires modeling work?

Question: In DynamoDB, you need atomic debit of account A and credit of account B. Why is 'two PutItems' insufficient?

Question: You adopt virtual threads for a servlet app, but a hot path still does `synchronized (mutex) { jdbc.call(); }`. Even if pinning is improved on newer JDKs, what remains the staff-level problem?
